chapter: The Parliamentary System: Legislature and Executive
name: Composition of the Parliament of India

scenes.animation: A school bus of Grade 8 students pulls up at the new Parliament building in Delhi. Zippy zooms around its soft triangular outline, tracing it with a glowing trail, while carvings of peacocks, lotuses and the Ashokan emblem shimmer on the walls.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: It's not square, it's not round. Is it a samosa?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Ha! It's a soft triangle. The three-sided design reflects balance, inclusivity and purpose.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It even uses green construction to cut electricity use by 30 per cent.

scenes.animation: A split screen: the old circular building labelled 'Samvidhan Sadan, built 1920s' and the new 'Sansad Bhavan'. A counter ticks from '1st Lok Sabha, 1952' to '18th Lok Sabha, June 2024'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The people of India directly elect members of the Lok Sabha. A majority group among them forms the government.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Parliament is the supreme law-making body. It controls and guides the work of the government, so the government works with the people's consent.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The 18th Lok Sabha was constituted in June 2024.

scenes.animation: A diagram builds step by step: a box 'Parliament of India' splits into three parts: 'President', 'Lok Sabha: House of the People, Lower House' and 'Rajya Sabha: Council of States, Upper House'. The word 'bicameral' splits into 'bi = two' and 'cameral = chamber'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Parliament is made up of the President and two Houses: the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A structure with two Houses is called bicameral. 'Bi' means two, and 'cameral' means chamber.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Why two Houses? Isn't one enough?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Constitution makers felt one directly elected House would not be enough. In the spirit of federalism, a Council of States was needed too.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Federalism means power is shared between the centre, the states and local governments.

scenes.animation: Inside the Lok Sabha chamber, a Speaker taps a gavel as members raise hands. In the Rajya Sabha, the Vice President sits in the chair. A golden sceptre with Nandi on top, labelled 'Sengol', glows beside the Speaker's chair.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Each House has a presiding officer. Lok Sabha members elect a Speaker, who runs sessions and maintains discipline.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Rajya Sabha is presided over by the Vice President of India, as its chairperson.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Near the Speaker's chair stands the Sengol, a sceptre from the Chola period. It was handed to Jawaharlal Nehru on 14 August 1947 to mark the transfer of power.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: the Speaker presides over the Lok Sabha, but the Vice President presides over the Rajya Sabha. Don't mix them up.

scenes.animation: Speech bubbles in many Indian scripts float around the chamber. A counter shows '12 languages' and then '+6 more', as tags appear: Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Manipuri, Urdu, Sanskrit.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: To make debates accessible, interpretation was available in 12 languages. Six more were added recently, including Bodo, Dogri and Sanskrit.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So a member can speak in their own language and everyone understands? Cool!

scenes.animation: Recap board with a triangular Parliament icon. Points appear: '1. Parliament = President + Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha', '2. Bicameral: two Houses, for federal balance', '3. Speaker presides over Lok Sabha; Vice President over Rajya Sabha'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: the Parliament is made up of the President, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: India has a bicameral Parliament, with the Rajya Sabha representing the states.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: the Speaker presides over the Lok Sabha, and the Vice President over the Rajya Sabha.

chapter: The Parliamentary System: Legislature and Executive
name: Legislative Functions: How a Bill Becomes a Law

scenes.animation: A cartoon rolled-up document with a face and a name tag 'RTE' walks into the frame, carrying a school bag. Zippy stares at it.

lines.speaker: RTE
lines.text: Hello! I'm the Right to Education Act. It took me almost a century to become a law!

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: A hundred years? I thought laws were just written overnight!

scenes.animation: Four boxes appear one by one under the heading 'Functions of Parliament': '1. Constitutional functions', '2. Lawmaking', '3. Executive accountability', '4. Financial accountability'. The first box opens to show icons for electing the President and amending the Constitution.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Parliament has four key functions: constitutional functions, lawmaking, executive accountability and financial accountability.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Constitutional functions include electing the President and Vice President, and amending the Constitution.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Parliament also upholds core values like universal adult suffrage, separation of powers, federalism, and Fundamental Rights.

scenes.animation: A timeline builds left to right as RTE walks along it: 'Roots in Directive Principles', 'Early 1990s: court case links education to Right to Life', '2002: 86th Amendment adds Article 21A, ages 6 to 14', '2008: tabled as a bill in the Rajya Sabha', 'August 2009: passed, President's assent'.

lines.speaker: RTE
lines.text: My roots lie in the Directive Principles of State Policy.

lines.speaker: RTE
lines.text: In 2002, the 86th Constitutional Amendment added Article 21A: free and compulsory education for all children from 6 to 14 years.

lines.speaker: RTE
lines.text: Six years later, I was tabled as a bill in the Rajya Sabha. A committee studied me, and in August 2009, I was passed in the Lok Sabha and got the President's assent.

scenes.animation: A flowchart builds step by step, each box lighting up as a paper bill slides through: 'Introduction in either House' then 'Reading of the bill' then 'Referred to Standing Committee' then 'Clause-by-clause discussion and amendments' then 'Vote on the bill' then 'Process repeated in other House' then 'Presidential assent' then 'Gazette notification'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A bill is a draft of a proposed law. It is introduced in either House and read.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It may be sent to a Standing Committee, a permanent committee of MPs that studies it.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Then it is discussed clause by clause, amended and voted on. The same process happens in the other House.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Finally, the President gives assent, and it is published in the Gazette, the official government publication.

scenes.animation: A bill stamped 'Money Bill' tries to enter the Rajya Sabha door, but a sign reads 'Lok Sabha only'. It turns around and enters the Lok Sabha after receiving a small 'Recommended by the President' stamp.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Can every bill start in either House?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Not every bill. A Money Bill, about taxes or government borrowing, can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, with the President's prior recommendation.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: learn the steps from bill to act in order. Drawing this flowchart neatly can earn easy marks.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a scroll turning into a stamped law book. Points appear: '1. Four functions: constitutional, lawmaking, executive and financial accountability', '2. Bill: introduction, reading, committee, clauses, vote, other House, assent, gazette', '3. Money Bills start only in the Lok Sabha'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: Parliament's four functions are constitutional, lawmaking, executive accountability and financial accountability.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: a bill passes through both Houses, gets the President's assent and a gazette notification to become an act.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: Money Bills can start only in the Lok Sabha.

lines.speaker: RTE
lines.text: And that's how I got every child a seat in school!

chapter: The Parliamentary System: Legislature and Executive
name: Accountability and the Union Executive

scenes.animation: A school canteen: the canteen manager stands before a table of students who fire questions: 'Why is the samosa cold?', 'Where did the money go?'. The scene morphs into a minister standing up in the Lok Sabha during 'Question Hour'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Why is everyone grilling that minister?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It's Question Hour. In a democracy, those who run the government must answer questions.

scenes.animation: A diagram builds: 'Union Executive' splits into 'President', 'Vice President' and 'Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister'. An arrow labelled 'answerable' points from the Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Making laws is the legislative function. Making sure laws are implemented is the executive function.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Union Executive is the President, the Vice President and the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Ministers are chosen from MPs of both Houses, and they are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.

scenes.animation: A clock shows the first hour of the session with the label 'Question Hour'. Then a committee room appears where officials from a ministry answer MPs across a table. Finally, a big budget folder is passed around, with coins flowing to different ministry boxes.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In Question Hour, usually the first hour of a sitting, MPs ask ministers about government policies. This keeps the executive accountable.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Committees also question ministries about their work.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: For financial accountability, Parliament approves and monitors spending through the annual budget.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Of course! It's the people's money, so someone must check it.

scenes.animation: Two figures stand side by side: the President with a crown-like label 'Head of State, nominal head' and the Prime Minister with a steering wheel labelled 'de facto executive'. Four task cards orbit the Prime Minister: 'Leads Council of Ministers', 'Coordinates ministries', 'Advises the President', 'Shapes national policies'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The President is the Head of State and the nominal head of the executive. The President appoints the Prime Minister and ministers, summons Parliament and gives assent to bills.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In a political crisis, like when no party has a clear majority, the President can use discretionary powers.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Prime Minister is the de facto executive authority. The President appoints the leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha as Prime Minister.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Civil servants help ministers implement laws and policies.

scenes.animation: A sepia flashback to 1956: a train accident headline, then Lal Bahadur Shastri handing a resignation letter across a desk. A label reads 'Moral responsibility'. An 'Exam Tip' sticker pops up beside the words 'nominal head' and 'de facto head'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1956, Railway Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri resigned after a train accident, though he was not blamed. He believed a minister must take moral responsibility.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: the President is the nominal head, but the Prime Minister is the de facto, or real, executive head. This is asked often.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a question-mark microphone and a budget folder. Points appear: '1. Executive = President, Vice President, Council of Ministers led by PM', '2. Question Hour and committees keep ministers accountable', '3. President: nominal head; PM: de facto head'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: the Union Executive is the President, the Vice President and the Council of Ministers led by the Prime Minister.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: Question Hour, committees and the budget keep the executive accountable to Parliament.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: the President is the nominal head, and the Prime Minister is the real executive head.

chapter: The Parliamentary System: Legislature and Executive
name: Legislature, Executive and Judiciary: Checks and Balances

scenes.animation: A cricket match where one player is batting, bowling and also umpiring. Zippy, as the fielder, throws up his hands. The scoreboard reads 'Unfair!'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: He's the batter, the bowler and the umpire? That's not fair!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exactly. That's why a democracy never gives all the power to one organ.

scenes.animation: A two-column table builds row by row, 'Legislature' on the left in blue and 'Executive' on the right in orange: 'Makes laws, oversees executive' vs 'Enforces laws'; 'Asks questions, seeks explanations' vs 'Gives information and explanations'; 'Sanctions expenses' vs 'Prepares and implements budget'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The legislature makes laws and oversees the executive. The executive enforces those laws.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Most bills are introduced by the executive, but the legislature keeps a check by asking questions and seeking explanations.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The legislature sanctions all government expenses, while the executive prepares and implements the budget that Parliament approves.

scenes.animation: Zippy points at a minister who sits in the Lok Sabha and also heads a ministry office; a dotted line connects both seats. Neo draws a line between 'making laws' and 'running the government', with the Lok Sabha holding a leash labelled 'accountability'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Hold on. Ministers are MPs too. So how are the legislature and executive separate?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Good catch! Ministers sit in Parliament, but their roles are different. As the executive, they run the government day to day.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: And the legislature can still question them, and they must answer to the Lok Sabha.

scenes.animation: A third pillar labelled 'Judiciary' rises beside the other two, holding a copy of the Constitution. A law scroll from the Parliament passes under its magnifying glass and gets a green tick; another scroll gets a red flag reading 'Violates Constitution'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The judiciary interprets and applies the laws and resolves disputes through a system of courts.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It is the custodian of the Constitution. It checks that laws passed by Parliament do not violate the Constitution.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: If the executive violates the Constitution while implementing a law, the judiciary can step in too.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So the judiciary is the third umpire!

scenes.animation: Three pillars, Legislature, Executive and Judiciary, hold up a roof labelled 'Democracy'. Arrows loop between them showing each checking the others. The phrase 'Separation of powers + checks and balances' writes itself across the roof.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: This is the separation of powers, with a system of checks and balances.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Each organ watches the others, so that no one organ becomes too powerful, and citizens' rights stay protected.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: in one line, the legislature makes laws, the executive implements them, and the judiciary ensures they follow the Constitution.

scenes.animation: Recap board with three pillar icons. Points appear: '1. Legislature makes laws and checks the executive', '2. Executive enforces laws and answers to the legislature', '3. Judiciary guards the Constitution; no organ is too powerful'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: the legislature makes laws and keeps a check on the executive.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: the executive enforces laws and must explain its actions to the legislature.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: the judiciary guards the Constitution, so no organ becomes too powerful.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Batter, bowler, umpire: three different people. Fair game!

chapter: The Parliamentary System: Legislature and Executive
name: State Legislatures and Challenges Ahead

scenes.animation: Zippy stands in front of the grand Vidhana Soudha building in Karnataka, then zooms back to the Parliament in Delhi, looking between the two.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Wait, states have their own Parliament too?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Kind of! Each state has its own legislature and executive, built like a mini version of the Union.

scenes.animation: Three circles appear: 'Union List' (Parliament), 'State List' (state legislature) and an overlapping 'Concurrent List' in the middle with icons for education and environment. The RTE character stands in the overlap, with an arrow showing the Union law applying all over India.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Constitution divides subjects into lists. Parliament makes laws on the Union List, and states on the State List.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: On the Concurrent List, both can make laws. But if the Union legislates on it, the state must follow.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Education is on the Concurrent List, yet the RTE Act applies all over India.

scenes.animation: A mirror-image table builds row by row: 'President' mirrors 'Governor, appointed by the President'; 'Prime Minister' mirrors 'Chief Minister'; 'Lok Sabha' mirrors 'Vidhan Sabha'; 'Rajya Sabha' mirrors 'Vidhan Parishad, some states only'. An India map highlights six states: Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The state structure mirrors the Union. The Governor, appointed by the President, is the nominal head. The Chief Minister is the real executive head.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Vidhan Sabha, the legislative assembly.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Only six states have two Houses, with a Vidhan Parishad: Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh. The rest are unicameral.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: learn these six bicameral states for map and short-answer questions.

scenes.animation: A calendar shows three session blocks: 'Budget', 'Monsoon', 'Winter'. A bar chart of Lok Sabha sittings shrinks: 1st Lok Sabha 677, 2nd 567, 10th 423, 13th 356. Storm clouds labelled 'disruptions' and 'absenteeism' hover over an empty chamber.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Parliament usually meets in three sessions a year: Budget, Monsoon and Winter.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: But the number of sittings has fallen, from 677 in the first Lok Sabha to 356 in the thirteenth.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Absenteeism, disruptions of Question Hour and poor-quality debates are serious challenges.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So how do we fix it?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Citizens can stay informed, join public discussions and engage with their representatives.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a Union building and a state building side by side. Points appear: '1. Union, State and Concurrent Lists divide lawmaking', '2. Governor and Chief Minister mirror President and Prime Minister', '3. Informed citizens help legislatures work better'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: the Union, State and Concurrent Lists decide who makes laws on what.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: in states, the Governor is the nominal head and the Chief Minister is the real head.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: informed, engaged citizens help our legislatures work better.
